title: The acrobats
hook: protecting yourself you protect others; protecting others you protect yourself (SN 47.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: vedana, and your line, let's look after you. Did you meet someone's illness, or your own, with care instead of blame? Day three hundred seventy-five.

Long ago, the Buddha tells his monks, an acrobat sets up a tall bamboo pole and calls to his apprentice, Medakathalika: climb the pole and stand on my shoulders. She does. Then he says the sensible-sounding thing. You look after me, and I'll look after you. That way we'll show our skill, collect our fee, and get down safely. And from up on his shoulders, she says no. The Buddha is staying near a town called Sedaka when he tells this story, and he takes her side. Today: the acrobats.
screen: `A BAMBOO POLE.` → `YOU WATCH ME, I'LL WATCH YOU.` → `FROM HIS SHOULDERS: NO.`

segments.voice: Here's her answer. That's not the way, master. You protect yourself, and I'll protect myself. Guarded and protected like that, we'll show our skill, collect our fee, and come down safely. And the Buddha says: that's the method. It sounds backward at first. Isn't looking after each other the kind thing? But picture it. She's high up on his shoulders, trying to watch his feet. He's balancing a pole while trying to watch her. Both of them are looking at the wrong thing. If each keeps their own balance, the whole act holds. Then the Buddha turns the picture into a teaching with two sides. Protecting yourself, you protect others. How? By practicing mindfulness, developing it, making much of it. A steady person is safer to be around. Protecting others, you protect yourself. How? By patience, by harmlessness, by loving-kindness, by care. A kind person lives with fewer enemies. So it isn't selfish against selfless. It's one movement, seen from two directions. That's why this sits beside right action. Someone off balance can't hold anyone up for long, and someone who harms others is never really safe. Consider the person in a family or an office everyone leans on. The best thing they can give the people on their shoulders may be their own steadiness.
screen: `YOU PROTECT YOU; I'LL PROTECT ME.` · `EACH KEEPS THEIR OWN BALANCE.` · `GUARDING YOURSELF GUARDS OTHERS.` · `GUARDING OTHERS GUARDS YOU.` · then, large: `THE ACROBAT'S BALANCE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, or sit tall. Feel your feet, or your seat, carrying your weight. Find your own balance: not rigid, just centered, with the small adjustments the body makes all by itself. Stay with that for a few breaths. Now think of one person who leans on you. Notice that your steadiness, right now, is already part of how you hold them. Then come back to your own center, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
The acrobats. Protecting yourself through mindfulness protects others; protecting others through patience and kindness protects you.
Your line: the acrobat's balance. Today, keep your own balance first, especially around someone who leans on you. Day three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the acrobat story to show that personal practice and care for others aren't in competition; many practitioners pair daily mindfulness with acts of patience and kindness.

match.prompt: who said what on the bamboo pole: tap the pairs.
pairs: you watch me, I'll watch you

myth: the Buddha sided with the master: watch each other
he says the apprentice has the method: each guards their own balance.
in this sutta, mindfulness is how you protect yourself
and patience, harmlessness, kindness and care are how you protect others.
the teaching treats guarding yourself and guarding others as opposites
it says each one leads to the other.

fork.setup: you're the apprentice, standing on the master's shoulders high on the bamboo pole. he says, "you watch me, I'll watch you." what do you say?
options: no: you protect yourself, and I'll protect myself.
fork.reveal: in SN 47.19 the apprentice says each should guard themselves, and the Buddha says she has the right method.

original.note: Pali: protecting oneself, one protects others.

trapdoor: what you thought: taking care of yourself first is selfish.
what it means: keeping your own balance keeps others safe, and caring for others keeps you safe.

what a scholar hears: SN 47.19 sits in the collection on the foundations of mindfulness: protecting oneself one protects others, by mindfulness; protecting others one protects oneself, by patience, harmlessness, mettā and sympathy.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01 (serious): the hook set the acrobats' performance in Sedaka, but in SN 47.19 Sedaka (a town of the Sumbhas) is where the Buddha is staying; the acrobat story is told as a tale from the past with no place named. Fixed. The 'market town' note above no longer applies.
SN 47.19 paraphrased. The apprentice's name Medakathālikā (feminine) follows modern translations; some readings treat the name differently. Confirm name and gender.
Sedaka is described in the sutta as a town of the Sumbhas; 'market town' is a loose gloss.
Pali line attānaṃ rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati, paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati: please confirm Devanagari.
The four ways of protecting others (khanti, avihiṃsā, mettā, anudayā): confirm.
